explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. One of His disciples says, "Lord, teach us to pray, just as John taught his disciples." (Luke 11:1). He doesn't ask for a miracle or a fancy speech. He asks about prayer, and I love that he just said it out loud.

Healing is a big thing, friend, but it's not what this disciple asks for. Luke 11:1 says he requested, "Lord, teach us to pray…" Jesus had just finished praying, and prayer is what the disciple brings up. I'd have forgotten my own question halfway through, so I'm impressed.

Fasting is a good guess, but this disciple doesn't ask about it. In Luke 11:1 he says, "Lord, teach us to pray…" That's the whole request, baker, plain and simple. Fasting will have to wait for a different passage.

Yes, baker. The disciple says, "…just as John taught his disciples." (Luke 11:1). He points at another teacher's students and basically asks for the same kind of lesson. I think that took some nerve, and I respect it. Asking plainly is a fine way to ask.
Elijah is a name people know, but this disciple doesn't use it. Luke 11:1 says, "…just as John taught his disciples." John is the teacher he names. Elijah can sit this one out.

Samuel's a fine name, friend, but it's not the one in this verse. The disciple asks Jesus to teach them "…just as John taught his disciples." (Luke 11:1). The name he says is John. I'll keep Samuel on the bench for a different passage.

I see why you'd go there, friend, because the prayer does talk about a kingdom. But Jesus says, "Father, hallowed be Your name. Your kingdom come." (Luke 11:2). The first word of the prayer itself is Father, and the kingdom comes after it. So this one is false.

That's right. Jesus tells them to say, "Father, hallowed be Your name. Your kingdom come." (Luke 11:2). The kingdom is in the prayer, but the first thing they call God is Father. That's a close one, baker, and you caught it.

You got it, baker. Jesus says, "Give us each day our daily bread." (Luke 11:3). The prayer asks for each day, one day at a time. That's like pulling one batch out of the oven at a time instead of worrying about a hundred batches at once. I could get used to that.

A week sounds nice and tidy, friend, but Luke 11:3 says, "Give us each day our daily bread." The word is day, not week. Picture me planning a whole week of cookie batches in one go, with the timer laughing at me. The prayer keeps it day-sized.

A year in one ask? That's a big order, baker. The prayer in Luke 11:3 says, "Give us each day our daily bread." It's a day-sized request. I tried counting a year of cookie boxes in my head once, and my mustache got tangled.

Yes, baker. The prayer says, "…for we also forgive everyone who sins against us." (Luke 11:4). The people asking God for forgiveness also say they forgive others. Forgiving is lighter to carry than a grudge, and I can tell you that from experience.

Warning people has its place, friend, but that's not what the prayer says. Luke 11:4 reads, "…for we also forgive everyone who sins against us." The word is forgive. Nobody in this prayer is handing out warning labels.

Dodging someone in the hallway is a real thing people do, baker. But the prayer doesn't go that way. It says, "…for we also forgive everyone who sins against us." (Luke 11:4). Forgive is the word Jesus gives them.

That's the one, baker. The prayer closes with, "And lead us not into temptation." (Luke 11:4). It comes right after the lines about bread and forgiveness, and it's a request about temptation. I think it's a handy one to pray when the cookie jar is wide open and nobody's looking.

Riches would be a nice add-on, friend, but they aren't in this prayer. It ends with, "And lead us not into temptation." (Luke 11:4). The last request is about temptation. I checked the whole prayer and found no wish list for treasure.

Enemies don't come up in the prayer, baker. Jesus ends it with, "And lead us not into temptation." (Luke 11:4). The last request is about temptation, so enemies aren't on the list. I read through every line of that prayer, and my mustache is tired from pointing.

Right on, baker. The man says, "because a friend of mine has come to me on a journey, and I have nothing to set before him." (Luke 11:6). A friend showed up from a trip, and he has nothing to set before him. I think that man was feeling the pressure. I'd have been sweating into my apron.

It's actually true, friend, and the story says so. The man tells his friend, "because a friend of mine has come to me on a journey, and I have nothing to set before him." (Luke 11:6). That's his reason for going to his friend at midnight. One guest, one journey, and nothing to set before him.
That's what he says, baker. The friend inside answers, "Do not bother me." (Luke 11:7). That's not exactly a warm greeting at midnight. I think I'd have been a little grumpy at that hour too.

What a nice neighbor that would be, friend, but those aren't his words. The friend inside answers, "Do not bother me." (Luke 11:7). Come on in isn't what he says first. I'd think twice before knocking on anybody's door at midnight.

Sending him down the street is a clever idea, baker, but that isn't what the friend says. His first words are, "Do not bother me." (Luke 11:7). The text doesn't have him point to another house. Those words are where his answer begins.

That makes sense as a guess, friend, but the man never says it. What he says is, "Do not bother me. My door is already shut, and my children and I are in bed. I cannot get up to give you anything." (Luke 11:7). He talks about the shut door and being in bed, and he says nothing about the bread running out. So this one is false.

You've got it, baker. The man inside says, "My door is already shut, and my children and I are in bed. I cannot get up to give you anything." (Luke 11:7). The door and the bed are his reasons, and he never says he's out of bread. Good catch on what the text leaves out.

Bingo, baker. Jesus says the friend will not get up "…because of his friendship, yet because of the man’s persistence, he will get up…" (Luke 11:8). The man keeps at it, and persistence is what Jesus names. It's like a cookie timer that keeps dinging until somebody finally walks over.

Money talks, friend, but it never gets a word in this story. Jesus says, "…because of the man’s persistence, he will get up…" (Luke 11:8). Nobody offers a payment anywhere in the passage. The persistence does the work.

Neighbors peeking through their curtains is a fun picture, baker, but they're not in the story. Jesus says, "…because of the man’s persistence, he will get up…" (Luke 11:8). The man's persistence is the reason, and the neighbors never come up.
That's what it says, baker. Luke 11:8 says he "…will get up and give him as much as he needs." The man asked for three loaves, and the friend gives what he needs. Not a crumb short.

One loaf would be a stingy ending, friend, but that's not what Jesus says. Luke 11:8 says the friend "…will get up and give him as much as he needs." The verse names the amount, and it's as much as the man needs. It doesn't count out a set number of loaves.

Half sounds like a bargain bin, baker, but that isn't what Jesus says. Luke 11:8 says the friend "…will get up and give him as much as he needs." The amount is tied to what the man needs, not to a fraction of his request. I'd call that a full tray, not half a tray.
That's the word, baker. Jesus says, "knock, and the door will be opened to you." (Luke 11:9). Ask, seek, knock, and the last one comes with a door. Easy to remember, even for a stamper.
Tapping on a window would get some strange looks, friend. Jesus says, "knock, and the door will be opened to you." (Luke 11:9). The word is door, not window. I'd stick to doors.
That one sounds big and holy, baker, but it isn't the word here. Jesus says, "knock, and the door will be opened to you." (Luke 11:9). The word is door. Heavens isn't in that line.

That's the one, baker. Jesus says, "For everyone who asks receives…" (Luke 11:10). Everyone is a big word, and it's the one He chose. He goes on to say that the one who seeks finds, and the door will be opened to him who knocks.

That would shrink the line a lot, friend, but Jesus doesn't say it. He says, "For everyone who asks receives…" (Luke 11:10). The word is everyone, with no list of who qualifies. That's good news for a stamper who spent years in a drawer.
Jesus is talking to His disciples here, baker, but listen to what He says. "For everyone who asks receives…" (Luke 11:10). The word is everyone, and it doesn't stop at the people in the room.

I get why it sounds that way, friend, but look at how Jesus puts it. He asks, "What father among you, if his son asks for a fish, will give him a snake instead?" (Luke 11:11). He asks it as a question about what a father would do, and He follows with the egg and the scorpion (Luke 11:12). He's not saying many fathers hand over harmful things, so this one is false.

That's right, baker. Jesus asks, "What father among you, if his son asks for a fish, will give him a snake instead? Or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion?" (Luke 11:11-12). He asks these as questions about what a father would do, and He never says fathers do it. That's a lot of animals for two questions.

That's what He says, baker. Jesus tells them, "…if you who are evil know how to give good gifts to your children…" (Luke 11:13). He says it plainly, and He doesn't dress it up. I'd have winced, but it sets up the best part right after.

It feels like a harsh thing to say, friend, but it's in the verse. Jesus says, "…if you who are evil know how to give good gifts to your children…" (Luke 11:13). He's honest about His listeners, and then He turns to what the Father does. So this one is true.

That's it, baker. Jesus says, "…how much more will your Father in heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him!" (Luke 11:13). He sets what fathers do with good gifts next to what the Father in heaven will do. What He names is the Holy Spirit, given to those who ask. When Jesus says how much more, I lean in like a stamper hearing the oven timer.

It's not just a tie, friend. Jesus says, "…how much more will your Father in heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him!" (Luke 11:13). Those words, "…how much more…", point past the fathers He's been describing. About the same isn't what He says.

That's not how Jesus says it, baker. He says, "…how much more will your Father in heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him!" (Luke 11:13). There's no "only sometimes" in the verse. It's "…how much more…"
You got it, baker. Jesus says, "…how much more will your Father in heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him!" (Luke 11:13). That's the gift He names at the end. Ask, and the Father gives.

Long life is a gift many would ask for, friend, but it isn't the one Jesus names. Luke 11:13 says the Father in heaven will "…give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him!" That's the gift He names at the end of the passage. I'll take the gift He actually names.

Great riches would be a fun answer, baker, but they're not here. Jesus says the Father in heaven will "…give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him!" (Luke 11:13). The Holy Spirit is the gift He names. I'll stick with that over a pile of treasure.
